title: Write a Playwright test that opens the app, navigates to login, enters credentials, submits, and asserts a successful login — and how do you make it robust (environment-specific base URLs, externalized test credentials/secrets, reused authentication state / storage state, Playwright auto-waiting instead of hard sleeps, and explicit negative/failed-login assertions)?
shortTitle: Writing a robust Playwright login test

s1_definition.profdef: A Playwright login test automates opening the application, navigating to the login page, entering credentials, submitting, and asserting the successful post-login state. Making it robust means not hard-coding the URL but reading an environment-specific base URL from configuration, never embedding credentials or secrets in the test but reading them from environment variables or a secret store, reusing a saved authentication storage state so most tests do not log in repeatedly, relying on Playwright's built-in auto-waiting through web-first assertions instead of fixed sleeps, and including explicit negative tests that assert a failed login shows the correct error and does not reach the dashboard.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a robot that logs into the National Bank of India app the same way Rajesh does: it opens the app, goes to the login screen, types the username and password, clicks sign in, and then checks that his dashboard appeared. To make this robot reliable, you do not glue the website address into it, you tell it which environment to use; you do not write Rajesh's real password in the script, you keep it in a safe place and hand it in at run time; you let the robot log in once and remember the signed-in state so the other hundred tests skip the login screen; you let the robot wait smartly for the page to be ready instead of blindly counting to five seconds; and you also teach it to try a wrong password and confirm the app correctly says "invalid credentials" and refuses entry.
s1_definition.oneliner: Write the login test to open, navigate, fill, submit, and assert the dashboard, and make it robust with an environment base URL, externalized secrets, reused storage state, Playwright auto-waiting web-first assertions instead of sleeps, and explicit failed-login negative assertions.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Playwright login test automates opening the application, navigating to the login page, entering credentials, submitting, and asserting the successful post-login state. Making it robust means not hard-coding the URL but reading an environment-specific base URL from configuration, never embedding credentials or secrets in the test but reading them from environment variables or a secret store, reusing a saved authentication storage state so most tests do not log in repeatedly, relying on Playwright's built-in auto-waiting through web-first assertions instead of fixed sleeps, and including explicit negative tests that assert a failed login shows the correct error and does not reach the dashboard.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a robot that logs into the National Bank of India app the same way Rajesh does: it opens the app, goes to the login screen, types the username and password, clicks sign in, and then checks that his dashboard appeared. To make this robot reliable, you do not glue the website address into it, you tell it which environment to use; you do not write Rajesh's real password in the script, you keep it in a safe place and hand it in at run time; you let the robot log in once and remember the signed-in state so the other hundred tests skip the login screen; you let the robot wait smartly for the page to be ready instead of blindly counting to five seconds; and you also teach it to try a wrong password and confirm the app correctly says "invalid credentials" and refuses entry.

**One line to remember:** Write the login test to open, navigate, fill, submit, and assert the dashboard, and make it robust with an environment base URL, externalized secrets, reused storage state, Playwright auto-waiting web-first assertions instead of sleeps, and explicit failed-login negative assertions.

sections.s2_technical:
The basic test drives the real browser: it navigates to the login page, locates the username and password fields with stable locators, fills them, clicks the submit button, and then asserts the successful outcome, typically that the URL changed to the dashboard and that a known post-login element such as a greeting or an account balance is visible. The assertion must target a reliable signal of success, not merely that the click happened.

Environment-specific base URLs keep the test portable across development, QA, staging, and production. Instead of hard-coding the address, you set a `baseURL` in the Playwright configuration, often read from an environment variable, and then navigate with a relative path, so the same test runs against any environment by changing one setting. This avoids the brittle anti-pattern of editing the test to point at a different server.

Externalized credentials and secrets are a security and maintainability requirement. You never commit usernames, passwords, or tokens into the test code or repository; instead you read them from environment variables injected by the CI secret store, or from a secure vault, so secrets never appear in source control and can differ per environment. Reused authentication state is a major robustness and speed technique: logging in through the UI is slow and flaky, so you perform the login once in a setup project, save the browser's cookies and local storage with `storageState`, and configure the rest of the tests to start already authenticated by loading that state. This means only a small number of tests actually exercise the login flow, while the bulk of the suite skips it, which is faster and far less flaky.

Auto-waiting instead of hard sleeps is central to Playwright's reliability model. Playwright's actions and its web-first assertions such as `expect(locator).toBeVisible()` automatically wait and retry until the condition is met or a timeout elapses, so you should never insert fixed sleeps like waiting two seconds, which are both slow, because they always wait the full time, and flaky, because they guess wrong under varying load. The negative tests are equally important: a robust login spec asserts not just that valid credentials succeed but that invalid credentials fail correctly, that the error message appears, that the user remains on the login page, and that no authenticated content is reachable, because in a bank the refusal path is as important as the success path. The senior nuances are to use role-based and label-based locators for stability, to keep one dedicated login test exercising the real flow while everyone else reuses storage state, to parameterize the base URL and secrets through configuration so nothing environment-specific or sensitive lives in the test, and to prefer Playwright's auto-waiting assertions everywhere so the suite is both fast and stable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India QA team must verify login works across four environments without editing the test, so the base URL must come from configuration. This is exactly the environment base-URL technique.

Problem 2 — Rajesh's credentials must never sit in the repository, and the hundred other tests should not each log in through the slow UI. This is exactly externalized secrets plus reused storage state.

Problem 3 — The suite must prove both that a valid login reaches the dashboard and that a wrong password is rejected with the right error and no access. This is exactly positive plus negative assertions with auto-waiting.

In the mini-project we provide a Playwright configuration with a base URL and a setup project that logs in once and saves storage state, a login page object, and a login spec with a positive test, a negative test, and a storage-state-reuse test. We write it in TypeScript as Playwright is a Node tool.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
bank-playwright/
├── package.json
├── playwright.config.ts          (baseURL, projects, storageState)
├── .env                          (NOT committed: secrets)
├── tests/
│   ├── auth.setup.ts             (logs in once, saves storage state)
│   ├── login.spec.ts             (positive + negative login tests)
│   └── dashboard.spec.ts         (reuses saved auth state)
├── pages/
│   └── LoginPage.ts              (page object with stable locators)
└── .auth/
    └── user.json                 (saved storageState, gitignored)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Install
npm init -y && npm i -D @playwright/test dotenv
npx playwright install

# Provide secrets + environment at run time (never commit these)
export BASE_URL=https://staging.nationalbank.example
export BANK_USER=rajesh
export BANK_PASS='Pass@123'

# Run all tests (setup logs in once, others reuse state)
npx playwright test

# Run only the login spec
npx playwright test tests/login.spec.ts

# Open the HTML report
npx playwright show-report
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a base URL from the environment, Rajesh's credentials from environment variables, and three specs, a setup login, a positive and negative login test, and a dashboard test that reuses state.

Step 1: The setup project runs first. It navigates to the relative login path, which resolves against the configured base URL, fills the username and password from environment variables, and submits.

Step 2: The setup waits with a web-first assertion for the welcome heading to be visible, with no fixed sleep, then saves the browser cookies and local storage to a storage-state file.

Step 3: The positive login test runs in its own context with empty storage state to exercise the real form, logs in, and asserts the URL became the dashboard, the welcome heading is visible, and the balance element contains the expected figure, all with auto-waiting.

Step 4: The negative login test submits a wrong password and asserts the alert shows the invalid-credentials message, the URL remains the login page, and no authenticated content element exists, proving the refusal path.

Step 5: The dashboard test runs in the authenticated project, loading the saved storage state, so it goes straight to the dashboard without touching the login screen, demonstrating reused authentication state for speed and stability.

Final output:

```
Running 4 tests using 2 workers
 [setup] authenticate (1.2s)
 [authenticated] dashboard shows balance without re-logging in (0.4s)
 login.spec.ts positive: valid credentials reach the dashboard (1.1s)
 login.spec.ts negative: invalid password is rejected and stays on login (0.9s)
  4 passed (4.0s)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  playwright.config.ts { baseURL from env, projects }
    │
    ▼
  [setup project] auth.setup.ts
    │ goto('/login') → fill(env user/pass) → submit
    │ expect welcome heading visible (auto-wait, no sleep)
    │ storageState() → .auth/user.json
    ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
  ▼                           ▼                             ▼
  login.spec (empty state)    dashboard.spec (uses state)   negative test
  real form → dashboard     goto('/dashboard')          wrong pass → error
  assert URL + balance        skips login UI (fast)          stays on /login, no balance
```

  [SETUP LOGIN] → [STATE SAVED] → [AUTH TESTS reuse state]
  [LOGIN SPEC] empty state → submit → [DASHBOARD] | [ERROR]

  ── Call Chain (positive) ───────────────────────────────

  2. login.login(user, pass)
  3. expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)
  4. expect(welcome heading).toBeVisible()

sections.s6_takeaway:
My Playwright login test opens the application, navigates to the login page, enters the credentials, submits, and then asserts a reliable success signal, that the URL became the dashboard and a known post-login element like the welcome heading and the account balance is visible, not merely that the click happened. But the interviewer is really asking how I make it robust, and I have five answers. First, the base URL is environment-specific: I set baseURL in the Playwright config from an environment variable and navigate with relative paths, so the same test runs against development, QA, staging, or production by changing one setting instead of editing the test. Second, credentials and secrets are externalized: I read the username and password from environment variables injected by the CI secret store, never committing them to the repository. Third, I reuse authentication state: I log in once in a setup project, save the cookies and local storage with storageState, and configure the rest of the suite to start already authenticated, so only a dedicated login test exercises the slow UI flow and the other tests skip it, which is dramatically faster and less flaky. Fourth, I rely on Playwright's auto-waiting: web-first assertions like expect locator toBeVisible automatically wait and retry, so I never insert fixed sleeps, which are both slow and flaky. Fifth, I include explicit negative assertions: a wrong password must show the correct error, keep the user on the login page, and leave no authenticated content reachable.

At the National Bank of India this structure mattered because we ran the suite against four environments and had over a hundred tests. Before I refactored it, every test logged in through the UI, which made the suite slow and intermittently flaky on salary-day load, and someone had even committed a test password. I introduced the setup-project storage-state pattern so login happened once, moved all secrets to the CI vault and environment variables, parameterized the base URL, replaced every fixed sleep with auto-waiting assertions, and added the failed-login negative test. The suite got faster and stopped flaking, and no secret lived in source control. Being able to write the basic test and then explain these five robustness techniques, environment base URL, externalized secrets, reused storage state, auto-waiting over sleeps, and negative assertions, is what shows an interviewer I write automation that survives in a real CI pipeline rather than a demo that only passes on my laptop.
